paragraph.text: hatred isn't an argument. Psychology helps explain where it usually comes from: people who don't eat meat go against a majority habit and are felt as a threat to values, traditions and identities, and meat eaters tend to put down vegetarians especially when they imagine being judged by them. It's an understandable defensive reaction, but it turns against people who, at bottom, are asking for less suffering for animals. And whatever anyone feels about vegans, the animals' suffering and death remain the issue.
L. Attacks on veganism and vegans ·
"I hate vegans. I can't stand people who don't eat meat."
Vegans, through what they say and do, morally condemn meat eaters and threaten habits, traditions and identities that many people value.
It's natural to feel aversion toward those who condemn us and threaten what we value.
If aversion toward a group is natural, there's no need to take what that group stands for seriously.
So I can reject vegans and what they stand for.

P1 has a true part: some vegans condemn others explicitly, and veganism does challenge a majority habit. P2 describes a real psychological reaction. The problem lies in P3: an emotional reaction says something about whoever feels it, but nothing about whether the rejected idea is true.
fails at P3, which swaps the assessment of the idea for a feeling about the people, and partly at P1, because much of the condemnation is anticipated rather than spoken.
"Vegans are the worst kind of people there is."
"I hate people who don't eat meat."
"Never trust someone who doesn't eat meat."
"Vegans are annoying and think they are better." (which is L1)

Imagine a classmate asks everyone to stop pulling the school dog's tail, because it hurts him. Someone might find the classmate annoying, or get angry at being corrected. But being angry at the classmate doesn't make the dog's pain go away. The question is still: is it right to hurt the dog?

I understand that many people feel judged, and some vegans really do speak aggressively. But psychology shows that much of this anger comes from feeling threatened: in a 2012 study, meat eaters rated vegetarians worse just after imagining how vegetarians would judge them. Hating people who ask for less suffering for animals doesn't answer what they're asking. You may not like me, and the animals keep suffering just the same.
"If no vegans existed, would what happens to the animals become right?"
The sentence offers no reason; it expresses a feeling about a group. But it's possible to reconstruct what it usually defends:
A habit and an identity that seem to be questioned
One's own moral self-image, which seems threatened
The majority norm, which the group goes against
A generalization that spares one from listening to any particular vegan
Feeling aversion toward a group says something about whoever feels it, but doesn't show the group is wrong. The question about the animals remains open.

text.bold: 2. Much of the anger is a defense against anticipated judgment.

paragraph.text: Minson and Monin showed in 2012 that meat eaters tend to put down vegetarians, and that simply asking people to imagine how vegetarians would judge them makes their ratings of vegetarians worse. In the first study, participants saw a small difference between the morality of meat eaters and that of vegetarians, but expected vegetarians to see it as almost ten times larger. The authors called this do-gooder derogation.

text.bold: 3. Vegans are felt as a threat to the status quo.

paragraph.text: MacInnis and Hodson proposed that people who abstain from meat go against the majority's values and are felt as a symbolic threat. In their study, omnivores rated vegetarians and vegans as negatively as or more negatively than several groups that are common targets of prejudice; only drug addicts were rated worse. Vegans were rated worse than vegetarians, and those who abstain for the animals or the environment were rated worse than those who do so for health.

Dhont and Hodson measured this threat with statements such as that eating meat is part of our cultural habits and identity, and showed that it helps explain why people with more right-wing ideologies are more accepting of animal exploitation. Rothgerber showed that, for many men, eating meat is tied to feeling masculine (L6). When a habit is part of who someone is, criticism of the habit is felt as criticism of the person.

text.bold: 5. The target of the hatred is whoever asks for less suffering.

paragraph.text: What veganism asks, in essence, is that animals not be made to suffer and die without need. Hating those who ask this doesn't answer the request; it turns a question about animals into a dispute about identity.

paragraph.text: 47% of participants associated at least one negative term with vegetarians; imagining being morally judged by them made ratings worse
Preprint of the article; samples of US undergraduates

paragraph.text: Omnivores rated vegetarians and vegans as negatively as or more negatively than several prejudice target groups; the bias was stronger among those with more right-wing ideologies, explained by perceived threat
The studies measure attitudes, not hatred; in the first study, participants weren't less willing to hire or rent to vegans

paragraph.text: Perceived threat from vegetarianism and belief in human supremacy help explain greater acceptance of animal exploitation and higher meat consumption
Men use more direct justifications for eating meat, and this use is related to masculinity

paragraph.text: People tend to prefer whatever option is already current, even when another would be as good or better
(d) The strongest counter-reply: vegans provoke the rejection they get

The most serious version says: hatred doesn't come from nowhere. Some vegans insult people, compare meat eaters to criminals and turn every meal into a sermon. People treated that way react, and the blame for the hostility lies, at least in part, with those who provoked it.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It explains part of the reaction, but not all of it.

paragraph.text: The studies show hostility appears even without any insult: imagining the judgment is enough. In Minson and Monin's study, participants were given no new information about vegetarians.
That some vegans insult people doesn't justify hating all of them, not even those who never said anything (L1).
Even if every vegan were unpleasant, what happens to the animals would stay the same. The form of the message can be criticized; the content needs an answer.

Liking vegans or not is a matter of feeling. The question they ask is a different one: is it just to make animals suffer and die when we don't need to? It doesn't depend on who asks it, or on how we feel about that person. Whatever one feels about vegans, the animals remain the issue.
L1 "Vegans are annoying and think they are better"
Irritation with the tone becomes hatred of the group
Meat becomes part of an identity to defend
Criticism of the form becomes rejection of the people
L3 "Vegans are crazy; they have mental problems"
L5 "Vegan activists are radicals and extremists"
E15 "I know it's wrong, but I won't change"
Without hatred as a shield, an admitted refusal is what remains
Ad hominem and poisoning the well
Rejects the idea because of who defends it
Uses a feeling instead of a reason
Judges all vegans by the worst examples
The feeling about vegans replaces the question about animals
But declares hatred of a whole group over a food choice.
But it's the hatred that ends the conversation.

text.bold: Doesn't hate people who defend dogs and cats.

paragraph.text: Whoever reports cruelty to a dog is usually admired, though they ask for something similar.
And hates precisely those who ask that animals not suffer.
Discrediting the vegan eases the moral judgment one imagines receiving
The vegan is felt as a threat to the majority's values and traditions
Criticism of the habit is felt as criticism of the person
The current habit seems right just for being current
The message is judged by dislike of whoever delivers it

text.link: Questão de Ética, vol. X, ch. 6

paragraph.text: The principle being tested is: "if I feel aversion toward those who defend an idea, I don't need to consider the idea".
Those who detested them could ignore slavery
They were widely vilified in their time, and they were right
People who report cruelty to dogs
Disliking the reporter would be enough to ignore the dog
Every moral question could be dismissed out of dislike
Morality would become a matter of personal taste

It's right that the feeling of being judged is real and uncomfortable, and that some vegans communicate aggressively, which makes dialogue harder. The movement should listen to this criticism, and those who defend animals gain by speaking respectfully. It's also right, unintentionally, in showing how closely food is tied to identity: that's why the conversation is hard.
But hatred doesn't answer the question; it only turns it into a dispute about who we are. And while people argue over whether vegans are bearable, the animals keep suffering and dying.
